newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Short Australia bonds make ready for FOMC.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Short Australia bonds make ready for FOMC.

text.p: *The short-end of the Australian debt market was easier in readiness for Tuesday's FOMC meeting, which is widely expected to endorse a 25 basis point U.S. interest rate hike.
*Analysts do not expect a re-run of the 1994 sell-off.
Short dated Australian bonds ended easier in readiness for Tuesday's Federal Open Market Committee meeting and the widely expected 25 basis point tightening in U.S. interest rates.
Long bonds yields, which were little changed on Monday, have risen by some 75 basis points in the past month, partly in anticipation of a U.S. rate rise.
However, analysts do not expect this to be the beginning of a re-run of 1994's massive sell-off when the Fed started its previous tightening cycle.
"This time, Australian bonds are not forecast to rise significantly more than U.S. Treasuries," said economists at ANZ Financial markets in a report.
In 1994, U.S. long bond yields rose 100 basis points during the first two months of rises in Fed funds, while local 10-year bonds jumped by 200 basis points.

ANZ said while much will depend on the pace of domestic growth and the risk to higher inflation, fundamentals in 1997 are pointing to more bond-friendly conditions. ANZ expects 3.5 percent growth at end-1997 compared with 3.1 percent at end-1996, and underlying inflation remaining at 2.1 percent.
"While the RBA will be forward looking, such an environment is unlikely to herald any particular rush on the part of the Reserve Bank to increase cash rates before 1998," ANZ said.
Analysts at HSBC markets also expect that there will be little local reaction to a 1/4 point U.S. interest rate rise and, unlike 1994, there could be a tightening in yield differentials to the U.S..
"Over the next few months, as the good news on inflation and on government budgets once again becomes prominent, we may even see a rally," said HSBC Markets' chief economist John Edwards.

Other than the FOMC meeting, the only major event locally in the short-term will be the possible release of the Industrial Relations Commission decision on the trade union movement's "living wage claim" this week.
The unions have sought three A$20 a week pay increases over the next three years and an 8.75 percent increase in minimum pay award rates this year. The government has proposed an A$8 a week increase.
A Reuters poll of economists on Friday expected just A$12 per week being awarded, and did not expect this to unduly concern the RBA in regard to future wage inflation growth.

Local bonds were outperformed by Canadian debt after comments by Finance Minister Paul Martin that he was confident that the Canadian economy could withstand a U.S. rate hike. BOC governor Gordon Thiessen also said that there was room for strong growth in coming quarters without impacting inflation.
